items.title: 7.1.7 Motion of a Free Particle Moving Along a Vertical Line

source_refs.note: Book p. 229: 7.1.7 free vertical motion, g = 9.8 m/s^2, replace a by g (down) or -g (up); Example 11 Free Fall from Rest and Example 12 Upward Throw

blocks.text: When a particle moves under the influence of gravity alone and air resistance is neglected, the motion is called free fall or free vertical motion. This motion takes place along a vertical straight line, either upward or downward. The acceleration due to gravity is denoted by \(g\) and is approximately:

blocks.text_alt: g equals 9.8 metres per second squared

blocks.text: If a particle is projected upward, its velocity decreases uniformly due to gravity and becomes zero at the highest point. If the particle moves downward, it accelerates toward the ground at the rate \(g\). The equations of motion for constant acceleration can also be used in vertical motion by replacing \(a\) with \(g\) for downward motion and with \(-g\) for upward motion.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\) means a falling body gains 9.8 m/s of speed every second (air resistance neglected), whatever its mass.
Sign rule: take the direction of motion as positive. Falling: gravity acts along the motion, \(a = +g\), speed increases. Rising: gravity acts against the motion, \(a = -g\), speed decreases until \(v = 0\) at the highest point. The table puts the two cases side by side.

rows: speed decreases, \(v = 0\) at the highest point
blocks.caption: Equations of motion with gravity, \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\) (our summary; positive direction = direction of motion)

blocks.title: Example 11
blocks.problem: (Free Fall from Rest) A stone is dropped from the top of a tower 45 m high. Find the time taken to reach the ground and the final velocity on impact.
steps:
Given: \(u = 0\), \(x = 45\) m, \(a = g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\).
To find: the time \(t\) to reach the ground and the final velocity \(v\) on impact.
Method: \(u\), \(x\), \(a\) are known and \(t\) is wanted, so use \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\); then \(v = u + gt\).

Use the equation of motion
\[x = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}\]
Substitute values:
\[45 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^{2}\]
Why: "dropped" means released without a push, so \(u = 0\); the motion is downward, so \(a = +g\).

Solve for \(t\)
\[t = \sqrt{\dfrac{45 \times 2}{9.8}} \approx 3.03 \text{ s}\]
Why: \(t^{2} = \frac{90}{9.8} \approx 9.18\); time cannot be negative, so we take the positive root.

Final velocity on impact
To find the final velocity on impact, use the equation \(v = u + gt\). Substitute the known values:
\[v = 0 + 9.8 \times 3.03 \approx 29.7 \text{ m/s}\]
Why: the velocity grows by 9.8 m/s each second for about 3.03 s.

Check:
\[v^{2} = u^{2} + 2gx = 2 \times 9.8 \times 45 = 882\]
\[v = \sqrt{882} \approx 29.7 \text{ m/s}\]
This does not use the rounded value of \(t\), and agrees.
blocks.answer: Time \(t \approx 3.03\) s; final velocity on impact \(v \approx 29.7\) m/s (downward).

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem: (Upward Throw) A ball is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 20 m/s. Find, the maximum height attained and the time to reach the maximum height.
steps:
Given: \(u = 20\) m/s, \(v = 0\) m/s (at top), \(a = g = -9.8\) m/s\(^2\).
To find: the maximum height and the time to reach it.
Method: at the highest point the ball stops for an instant, so \(v = 0\). First \(v = u + gt\) gives \(t\), then \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\) gives the height.

Time to reach the top
Use the equation of motion \(v = u + gt\). By substituting the values of \(u\), \(v\) and \(g\), we get:
\[0 = 20 + (-9.8)t\]
\[t = \dfrac{20}{9.8} \approx 2.04 \text{ s}\]
Why: the ball loses 9.8 m/s of speed each second, so losing 20 m/s takes \(\frac{20}{9.8}\) s. The value \(-9.8\) is used because gravity acts against the upward motion (see the correction below).

Maximum height
To find maximum height, use the equation of motion \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\). By substituting the values of \(u\), \(t\) and \(g\), we get:
\[x = 20 \times 2.04 + \dfrac{1}{2}(-9.8)(2.04)^{2}\]
\[\approx 20.4 \text{ m}\]
Why: \(20 \times 2.04 = 40.8\) and \(4.9 \times 2.04^{2} \approx 20.39\); \(40.8 - 20.39 \approx 20.4\).

Check:
\[2ax = v^{2} - u^{2}\]
\[2(-9.8)x = 0 - 400\]
\[x = \dfrac{400}{19.6} \approx 20.4 \text{ m}\]
Same height, found without using \(t\).
blocks.answer: Time to reach the maximum height \(t \approx 2.04\) s; maximum height \(\approx 20.4\) m.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
1. The question prints "Find, the maximum height"; the comma is a misprint: "Find the maximum height".
2. The solution writes \(a = g = -9.8\) m/s\(^2\) and then uses \(v = u + gt\) and \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\). But the book has just defined \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\) and said to replace \(a\) with \(-g\) for upward motion. Consistent form: \(a = -g = -9.8\) m/s\(^2\), so \(v = u - gt\) and \(x = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\). The numbers substituted (\(-9.8\)) are the same, so the answers 2.04 s and 20.4 m are correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Free fall: motion under gravity alone, air resistance neglected; \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\).
2. Use the equations of motion with \(a = g\) for downward motion and \(a = -g\) for upward motion.
3. "Dropped" means \(u = 0\); at the highest point \(v = 0\).
4. Time to the top \(= \frac{u}{g}\); maximum height \(= \frac{u^{2}}{2g}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the minus sign of \(g\) in upward motion, which makes the height far too large.
2. Thinking the acceleration is zero at the highest point: only the velocity is zero there.
3. Stopping at \(t^{2}\) and forgetting the square root.
4. Writing \(g = -9.8\) in one place and \(g = 9.8\) in another; keep \(g = 9.8\) and put the sign in the equation.
